Proficient = 8 of 10. Family agreement: complete, signed by child and parent.

weeks.prep: Parent preview: select 3 alcohol or tobacco ads from health-education collections (e.g., Stanford Tobacco Prevention Toolkit, historical ads at tobacco.stanford.edu) and one short TV or movie scene showing drinking or smoking that is appropriate for your child. Poster paper for the counter-ad.
misconceptions: Thinking ads show what really happens. Ads show glamour, fun and popularity and leave out health risks, addiction and cost.
Thinking influencer posts are just personal opinions. Many are paid (sponsored) posts; look for '#ad' or 'sponsored.'

days.guide: For each ad, identify the target audience and hidden messages (e.g., 'you'll be popular,' 'it's relaxing,' 'adults are cool'). Note what's missing (health effects, addiction).

questions.q: Who is the target audience of an ad with bright colors and cartoons?
questions.a: Young people.

questions.q: What do alcohol and tobacco ads usually leave out?
questions.a: Health risks, addiction, cost and real-life consequences.

days.guide: Watch the scene. Note how drinking or smoking is shown and whether consequences appear.

questions.q: Did the scene show any consequences? Why might media leave them out?
questions.a: Usually not; showing only the fun or glamorous side makes the product look appealing and makes the story simpler.

days.guide: Create a counter-ad that uses ad techniques to show the truth (e.g., 'Want yellow teeth, bad breath and a habit that costs thousands of dollars a year?').

questions.q: What makes a counter-ad effective?
questions.a: It grabs attention, uses true facts about the product's real effects, and targets the same audience.

days.guide: Discuss influencers and sponsored posts promoting vaping or products. Learn to look for '#ad,' 'sponsored,' or 'paid partnership.'

questions.q: What does '#ad' on a post mean?
questions.a: The influencer was paid or rewarded to promote the product.

days.guide: Write a media literacy checklist of questions for evaluating ads.

questions.q: Name 3 questions for your checklist.
questions.a: Who made this and why? Who is the target audience? What techniques are used? What is left out? Is it true? Is it paid?

weeks.assessment_key: Counter-ad and checklist rubric: 4 = counter-ad uses at least 2 attention techniques to present accurate facts about a real harm, targeted to a clear audience; checklist has at least 5 critical questions (who made it, purpose, audience, techniques, what's missing, sponsorship, accuracy); 3 = 3–4 questions or counter-ad with one fact; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Make 10 scenario cards (e.g., 'Friends say "Just try it, everyone does"' = spoken negative; 'Everyone at the table is on their phone so you get yours out' = unspoken; 'Your friend says "Come run with me"' = spoken positive). Health journal.
misconceptions: Thinking peer pressure is always spoken. Unspoken pressure — wanting to fit in because of what others are doing — is common too.
Thinking peer pressure is always bad. Positive peer pressure encourages healthy choices like studying, trying out for a team or being kind.

days.guide: Teach 4 kinds: spoken (direct asking, teasing, daring), unspoken (seeing others do something and wanting to fit in), positive (encourages healthy choices), negative (encourages unhealthy or unsafe choices). Give examples of each.

questions.q: What is unspoken peer pressure?
questions.a: Feeling you should do something because others are doing it, even though no one asked you.

questions.q: Give an example of positive peer pressure.
questions.a: E.g., a friend encourages you to join a sports team, try a new healthy food, or study for a test.

days.guide: Sort the 10 scenario cards by type and explain two choices.

questions.q: 'Your friends all wear a brand and you feel left out.' Which type?
questions.a: Unspoken (negative if it pushes you to do something you don't want).

questions.q: 'Come on, just one puff, don't be a baby.' Which type?
questions.a: Spoken, negative.

days.guide: List qualities of friends who support healthy choices (respect your no, encourage you, honest, kind, include you).

questions.q: How does a true friend respond when you say no?
questions.a: They respect your decision and don't keep pushing or tease you.

days.guide: Plan a way to use positive peer pressure for a healthy habit (e.g., invite friends to a bike ride instead of video games).

questions.q: How could you positively influence a friend?
questions.a: Model the healthy behavior and invite them to join, e.g., 'Let's play soccer at recess.'

days.guide: Write about a time you resisted pressure or helped someone else make a good choice.

questions.q: What strategies helped you resist?
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., saying no firmly, suggesting something else, leaving, being with supportive friends.

weeks.assessment_key: Peer pressure reflection rubric: 4 = describes a real situation, identifies the type of pressure (spoken/unspoken, positive/negative), explains the strategy used and the outcome, and what they learned; 3 = describes the situation and strategy; 2 = vague or no strategy; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Make a refusal skills card: 1) Say no clearly, 2) Give a reason, 3) Suggest something else, 4) Walk away (and tell a trusted adult if needed). Prepare scenario cards; the parent plays the pressuring peer gently. Scoring sheet for Friday.
misconceptions: Thinking you need a long excuse to say no. A firm 'No thanks' is enough; you don't owe an explanation.
Confusing assertive with aggressive. Assertive is clear and respectful; aggressive is rude, yelling or threatening.

days.guide: Act out passive (looking down, mumbling 'I don't know…'), aggressive (yelling, insulting) and assertive (eye contact, calm firm voice, standing tall, 'No, I don't want to') responses. Practice assertive voice and body language.

questions.q: Describe an assertive response.
questions.a: Standing tall, making eye contact, using a calm, firm voice and saying clearly what you want.

questions.q: What is the difference between assertive and aggressive?
questions.a: Assertive is firm and respectful; aggressive is hostile, loud or hurtful.

days.guide: Teach the 4 refusal steps and practice each with simple offers.

questions.q: What are the 4 refusal steps?
questions.a: Say no clearly, give a reason, suggest an alternative, walk away (and tell a trusted adult).

days.guide: Role-play: an older kid offers a vape. The child uses all 4 steps.

questions.q: Example refusal to a vape offer?
questions.a: 'No thanks. Vaping is addictive and I play soccer. Want to shoot some hoops instead?' Then walk away if they keep pushing.

days.guide: Role-play: someone offers alcohol at a party. The child refuses and calls a trusted adult to be picked up.

questions.q: What do you do if friends keep pressuring you at a party?
questions.a: Repeat no, leave the situation and call a parent or trusted adult to pick you up.

days.guide: New scenario (e.g., a friend offers a pill 'to help you stay awake'). The parent scores each step.

questions.q: Why is walking away an important step?
questions.a: It gets you out of the risky situation and ends the pressure.

weeks.assessment_key: Refusal skills performance check (score 1 point each, 6 total): says no clearly (1); gives a reason (1); suggests an alternative (1); walks away/leaves (1); assertive voice and eye contact (1); names a trusted adult to tell (1). 4 = 6; 3 = 5; 2 = 3–4; 1 = 0–2.

weeks.prep: Decision-making worksheet, pledge card, 3 ATOD scenarios (e.g., finding beer at a sleepover, a cousin offers a vape, a friend wants to take his sister's prescription pills). Prepare the Unit 9 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking a pledge alone keeps you drug-free. A pledge works best with a plan, healthy activities and supportive people.
Thinking stress requires a 'quick fix.' Healthy ways to manage stress include exercise, talking to someone, hobbies, rest and deep breathing.

days.guide: Apply the 5-step model (Stop, Think of options, Consider consequences, Choose, Check) to the 3 ATOD scenarios and write consequences for each option.

questions.q: A friend wants to take his sister's prescription pills. What is the healthy choice?
questions.a: Refuse, explain it's dangerous and illegal to take someone else's prescription, and tell a trusted adult.

questions.q: Name a consequence of saying yes to a vape.
questions.a: Nicotine addiction, harm to the developing brain, breaking family rules and the law, losing trust.

days.guide: List 10 healthy activities to have fun and manage stress.

questions.q: Name 3 healthy ways to manage stress.
questions.a: Any 3: exercise, talking with a trusted adult or friend, drawing or music, reading, deep breathing, getting enough sleep, spending time outside.

days.guide: Write a personal pledge with one specific action to keep it (e.g., 'I will leave any situation where people are using drugs and call my mom').

questions.q: Why add a specific action to your pledge?
questions.a: It gives you a plan for what to do, making it easier to keep the promise.

days.guide: Share the pledge with a trusted adult; discuss how they will support it.

questions.q: How can a trusted adult support your pledge?
questions.a: Being available to call, giving rides, talking about pressure, and praising good choices.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test (see key).

questions.q: Name the 4 refusal steps.
questions.a: Say no, give a reason, suggest an alternative, walk away.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key: 1) Name 2 types of peer pressure — spoken/unspoken or positive/negative. 2) Example of positive peer pressure — a friend encouraging you to join a team or study. 3) 4 refusal steps — say no, give a reason, suggest an alternative, walk away. 4) Assertive vs. aggressive — assertive is firm and respectful; aggressive is hostile. 5) 5 decision steps — Stop, Think of options, Consider consequences, Choose, Check. 6) Two media techniques used to sell tobacco/alcohol — e.g., glamour, celebrities, flavors, bright colors, 'everyone does it.' 7) What does '#ad' mean — paid promotion. 8) Two healthy ways to manage stress — exercise, talking to someone, hobbies, deep breathing. Proficient = 6 of 8. Pledge: written with a specific action and shared.

weeks.prep: Planning sheet (topic, audience, key message, 5 facts with sources, 2 products, timeline). Bookmark reliable sources: KidsHealth, MyPlate.gov, CDC, FDA 'The Real Cost,' NIDA for Teens.
misconceptions: Thinking any fact found online can be used. Facts must come from reliable sources and be written in your own words with the source named.
Trying to reach everyone with one message. Choose a specific audience and shape the message for them.

days.guide: Choose a topic (drink water, eat the rainbow, be active, stay vape-free) and explain why it matters to the child.

questions.q: Why choose a topic you care about?
questions.a: You'll be more motivated and your message will be more convincing.

days.guide: Identify the audience and what message and format will reach them (younger kids: pictures and songs; neighbors: flyers).

questions.q: How would your message change for younger kids vs. adults?
questions.a: Younger kids: simple words, pictures, fun; adults: facts, statistics and practical tips.

days.guide: Gather 5 facts from reliable sources and record each source.

questions.q: Is a fact from a company selling sports drinks a good source for a water campaign?
questions.a: No — it has a reason to be biased; use CDC, KidsHealth or MyPlate instead.

days.guide: Plan 2 products (poster, short video, flyer, skit) and sketch each.

questions.q: Why plan 2 different products?
questions.a: Different formats reach different people and repeat the message.

days.guide: Present the plan to a parent for feedback and revise.

questions.q: What feedback question could you ask?
questions.a: E.g., 'Is my message clear?' 'Would this convince you?'

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign plan rubric: 4 = clear topic and specific audience, a one-sentence key message, 5 accurate facts each with a reliable source, 2 planned products with sketches, and revisions from parent feedback; 3 = 4 facts or one missing element; 2 = vague audience or unreliable sources; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Poster paper, markers, a phone or tablet for video. Reliable source websites open for fact-checking.
misconceptions: Thinking a slogan must include all the facts. A slogan is short and catchy; the facts go on the poster or in the video.
Skipping fact-checking because the information 'sounds right.' Every number must match a reliable source.

days.guide: Write a short catchy slogan and a one-sentence key message. Test it on a family member: can they repeat it?

questions.q: What makes a good slogan?
questions.a: Short, catchy, easy to remember, and clearly connected to the healthy behavior (e.g., 'Sip Smart — Choose Water!').

days.guide: Create the poster: slogan, 3 facts with sources, a clear visual, and a call to action.

questions.q: Why include sources on the poster?
questions.a: So people know the facts are trustworthy and can check them.

days.guide: Record a 1-minute PSA video or rehearse a short skit that models the healthy behavior.

questions.q: Why model the behavior instead of just telling it?
questions.a: Seeing someone do it shows the audience how and makes it more memorable.

days.guide: Fact-check every statistic and claim against KidsHealth, MyPlate, FDA or NIDA; fix errors.

questions.q: You wrote 'Kids need 30 minutes of activity a day.' Is it correct?
questions.a: No — kids need at least 60 minutes a day (CDC). Correct it.

days.guide: Show materials to 2 people, collect one suggestion from each, and revise.

questions.q: What is one revision you made and why?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., 'I made the slogan bigger because my grandpa couldn't read it from far away.'

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign materials rubric: 4 = catchy slogan and key message; poster with slogan, 3 fact-checked facts with sources, strong visual and call to action; 1-minute video or skit that models the behavior; revisions from 2 people documented; 3 = all products with one weak element; 2 = missing a product or inaccurate fact; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Campaign materials, permission for a display location, a review game (e.g., Jeopardy-style board with categories Nutrition, Activity, Medicines, Tobacco/Vaping, Alcohol). Prepare the final assessment (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking health learning ends with the school year. Healthy habits and goals continue all summer and for life.
Thinking presenting means reading the poster aloud. Speak to the audience, make eye contact, and explain why the message matters.

days.guide: Present the campaign to family or a community group: introduce the topic, share the facts, show the products, and give the call to action.

questions.q: What should you do at the end of your presentation?
questions.a: Give the call to action and invite questions.

days.guide: Display posters (with permission) at home, a library, community center or co-op.

questions.q: Why ask permission before posting?
questions.a: To respect property and rules of the place.

days.guide: Play a review game covering nutrition, activity and ATOD.

questions.q: How many teaspoons of sugar in 24 g of sugar?
questions.a: 6 teaspoons (24 ÷ 4).

days.guide: Give the end-of-year assessment (see key).

questions.q: What does the 5/20 rule help you do?
questions.a: Decide whether a food is low (5% DV or less) or high (20% DV or more) in a nutrient.

days.guide: Write a reflection on the year's health goals and set a SMART summer goal.

questions.q: Give an example of a SMART summer goal.
questions.a: E.g., 'I will swim or bike for 45 minutes 4 days a week from June 15 to August 15 and track it on a calendar.'

weeks.assessment_key: Final assessment key (15): 1) 3 sides of health triangle — physical, mental/emotional, social. 2) 5 food groups — fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy. 3) Main job of protein — build and repair tissues. 4) 5/20 rule — ≤5% DV low, ≥20% DV high. 5) Best everyday drink — water. 6) 4 food safety steps — Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill. 7) Daily activity for kids — 60+ minutes. 8) Prescription vs. OTC — prescription needs a doctor's order for one person. 9) Poison Control — 1-800-222-1222. 10) Addictive drug in tobacco and vapes — nicotine. 11) Vape aerosol is not just water vapor; name one thing in it — nicotine, heavy metals, ultrafine particles, flavor chemicals. 12) Alcohol is a — depressant. 13) Organ that breaks down alcohol — liver. 14) 4 refusal steps — say no, give a reason, suggest an alternative, walk away. 15) Legal age for alcohol/tobacco in CA — 21. Proficient = 12 of 15. Campaign presentation rubric: 4 = clear, confident delivery with eye contact, accurate sourced facts, call to action; 3 = clear with minor issues; 2 = reads from notes, few facts; 1 = incomplete.
